steps.observation: You have 30 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The storms had been getting stranger.

Elias could tell by the way the light behaved. The beam from his lighthouse used to carve a clean white path across the black Atlantic, steady as a metronome. Lately, it flickered when the sky was clear and burned unwavering during gales that should have rattled the glass from its panes.

He lived alone on the rock, six miles from the mainland, with a radio that coughed static and a kettle that screamed louder than any foghorn. Each evening he climbed the spiral stairs, lit the lamp, and watched the horizon until his eyes ached.

One night, the sea went utterly calm—flat as poured oil. No wind, no waves. The beam swept in its patient circle, and Elias noticed something impossible: a figure standing on the surface of the water, just beyond the edge of the light.

He blinked. The figure remained, a dark seam against the dim glow.

He turned up the lamp, forcing the beam out further. The figure resolved into the suggestion of a coat, a hat, the glint of eyes. Not a man, exactly, but the idea of one, as if the ocean were trying to remember how people looked.

The radio crackled behind him. A woman’s voice, thin and far away, threaded through the static.

“Keep it steady,” she said. “We’re still out here.”

Elias swallowed. No ships had passed in weeks. The shipping lanes had moved years ago, and this lighthouse was kept more from nostalgia than necessity.

“Who are you?” he asked the empty air, but the radio only hissed.

When he looked back, the figure had moved closer. Each sweep of the light found it a few yards nearer, though it made no motion he could see. The ocean, perfectly smooth, did not ripple.

Elias felt an old fear uncoil in his chest: not of storms, but of finally having nothing at all to save.

He remembered his father’s hands guiding his on the lamp’s brass fittings, the smell of oil and salt. “Our job,” his father had said, “isn’t just for the ones who are coming. It’s for the ones who never made it. You owe them the light.”

The figure reached the base of the rock.

Elias could have doused the lamp. Closed the shutters, hidden in the stairwell like a child. Instead, he opened the service door and stepped out into the salt-thick air. The night pressed close, the only sound his own blood in his ears.

Below, at the bottom of the cliff, the figure stood on the black surface of the sea, directly in the path of the beam. As the light washed over it, its edges softened, as if it were made of mist held together by will alone.

“You kept it burning,” it said, voice carrying with no wind to help it. “Even when they said there was no point.”

Elias gripped the railing. “There’s always fog,” he said, because he couldn’t think of anything else.

The figure gave a small, almost human laugh. “Yes. There is always fog.”

The radio flared again behind him, filled now with layered voices—men and women, young and old, overlapping like waves on rock:

“Starboard—”
“—couldn’t see a thing—”
“—there, there’s the light—”

They rose and fell, a collage of near-misses and last hopes, all of them pinned to this one bright spinning point. Elias’ throat tightened.

“Are you… them?” he asked.

The figure tilted its not-quite-head. “We’re what remains of them when the sea is done,” it said. “Memory needs somewhere to shine from.”

“Why come now?” Elias said. “After all these years?”

The horizon shimmered. For a moment he saw shapes that were not ships at all: wooden hulls long rotted, iron ribs cracked by ice, names worn away. All of them facing the rock, like flowers turning toward the sun.

“Because they’re thinking of closing you,” the figure answered. “Taking your lamp. Leaving the rock dark.”

Elias thought of the letters—budget cuts, automation, satellite beacons. “I can’t stop them.”

“No,” the figure agreed. “But you can be here. Until the last night.” It paused. “We wanted you to know it mattered.”

The wind returned in a sudden, sharp gust, flinging salt spray against his face. When he blinked it away, the figure was gone. The sea chopped itself back into waves, indifferent and loud.

Inside, the radio had gone silent.

For the first time in years, Elias sat in the gallery all night, back against the glass, watching the light complete its endless circles. Somewhere beyond the horizon, cargo ships and fishing boats passed, guided now more by satellites than by the old beam. Still, the lamp arced across dark water, catching on whitecaps, on distant rain, on nothing at all.

At dawn, he brewed tea and stood at the window. The ocean looked ordinary again. He felt older and strangely lighter.

They would come one day with their paperwork and their polite apologies, and the lamp would be switched off, the lens shrouded. The rock would return to being only a rock.

Until then, Elias climbed the stairs each evening and lit the lamp with careful, practiced hands.

He kept it steady.
